name: Imagine Math
line: Imagine Math places by test, then teaches by the lesson. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are at every problem.
description: AMP vs Imagine Math: Imagine Math places by test and teaches in lessons that end in a quiz. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous.
verdict: Imagine Math places a student with a placement assessment, then moves them along a pathway of lessons, each ending in a quiz [2][3]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Imagine Math builds a pathway of lessons from a placement assessment, and benchmark tests return during the year [1][2].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step and never the answer, a written lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer after it is answered, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Imagine Math the unit is the lesson: a string of interactive activities with scaffolded feedback, ending in a quiz [2][3]. From grade 3, help also comes from live sessions with a teacher [1]. A meta-analysis of 55 studies found that worked examples improve mathematics performance [7].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP an answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. A skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. In Imagine Math a lesson counts as passed at 75% or better on the quiz at its end, in the studies we read [2][5]. A student's goal is set in lessons passed [1].

reasons.title: What the adult does
reasons.body: In AMP the adult does not plan, teach or grade. Parents and teachers see a level for each part of math and the actual problems behind every number, and each lesson has a guide for the adult. Imagine Math is built for a teacher who assigns work, reads class and student reports, and plans differentiated teaching [1].

theirs: Imagine Math is a supplemental math program from Imagine Learning, designed to support and extend classroom instruction [2]. It runs from pre-kindergarten through Geometry [3].

A student starts with a placement assessment that builds a pathway of lessons [2]. Each lesson strings together interactive activities with scaffolded feedback and ends in a quiz [2][3]. Benchmark tests during the year track a Quantile measure, and from grade 3 a student can reach live help sessions with a teacher [1]. A teacher assigns work, reads the reports and plans differentiated teaching [1].
credit: From grade 3, a student can reach a live teacher for help from inside a lesson [1].
Its placement and benchmark tests report a Quantile measure and a percentile rank [1].
It has been studied in matched comparisons, including a Johns Hopkins University evaluation in Idaho [2][4].

theirs: Evidence for ESSA, run by Johns Hopkins University, rates Imagine Math Promising, on two matched-comparison studies with an average effect size of +0.06 [4]. One is the charter-network study described below (+0.08). The other, by RMC Research in Indiana and Texas, was significant only for Indiana grades 3 to 5 (+0.13) [4]. Both compare students who used the program with similar students who did not. We found no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report on Imagine Math and no randomized trial of it.

A Johns Hopkins University team evaluated Imagine Math in Idaho with the state education department and Imagine Learning, and Imagine Learning posted the report [2]. It is not one of the two studies behind the rating, and the report does not name a funder. It matched 17,226 users in grades 4 to 8 with 17,226 similar non-users and compared spring 2025 state test scores. Finishing one lesson counted as use. Users scored 5.21 points higher, an effect size of 0.04. Grades 4 and 7 reached 0.06, and students in special education 0.10. Students who passed 30 or more lessons scored 0.08 above matched peers, a link that does not show cause [2].

A study published by Imagine Learning in a charter network in Florida and North Carolina found g = 0.078 on MAP Growth for 9,015 users against matched non-users. Imagine Math was used at teachers' discretion, and users passed 21.2 lessons in 17.6 hours on average [3]. A company brief from one California district compares heavier users with lighter users, which cannot show cause [5].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. A meta-analysis of 55 studies found that worked examples improve mathematics performance, with an average effect of g = 0.48 [7]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [6]. AMP gives a worked example with every problem and brings learned skills back mixed with other math.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: You want a student to be able to reach a live teacher for help from inside a lesson.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no placement or benchmark tests.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want a skill to count only when your child gets it right without help, more than once.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math, or headed past Geometry.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Imagine Math?
questions.answer: Imagine Math places a student with a placement assessment and moves them along a pathway of lessons, each ending in a quiz [2][3]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Imagine Math work?
questions.answer: Evidence for ESSA rates it Promising, on two matched-comparison studies averaging +0.06 [4]. In a Johns Hopkins University evaluation of 34,452 Idaho students, users scored 0.04 standard deviations above matched non-users [2]. We found no randomized trial of Imagine Math.

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers and chooses practice from there.
